item.title: Google Researcher Uses AI Agents to Find Maya Site, Then Discovers It Was Already Known
item.description:
Google Researcher Uses AI Agents to Find Maya Site, Then Discovers It Was Already Known

Google researcher Pietro Miotti recently claimed to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico using AI agents and lidar technology. However, subsequent verification revealed the site had already been documented in an academic journal.

🔍 Overview

  • Researcher: Pietro Miotti, a Google researcher.
  • Goal: To find undocumented Maya sites in Mexico.
  • Initial Finding: A major village that appeared not to be registered in existing records.
  • Government Response: Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) confirmed they had no record of a registered site at that location.
  • Correction: The site was already discovered and published in an academic journal more than a year earlier.

🤖 Methodology

  • Technology: Lidar (laser-based mapping) to produce detailed three-dimensional images.
  • Agents: A team of 48 AI agents.
  • Data Source: NASA lidar data.
  • Process: Agents combed through data for signs of undocumented sites and translated correspondence into Spanish.
  • Timeline: The process took less than 72 hours from a random thought to an official government reply.

⚠️ Verification and Correction

  • Misconception: Miotti noted that not being registered in a database does not mean a site has not been mapped.
  • AI Limitations: Miotti stated, “My agents and I missed it.” He added that he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped.
  • Verification Process: Archaeologists do not publish the coordinates of sites. Therefore, checking whether a site is already known requires comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database.

💡 Expert Perspectives

  • Sarah Parcak: Stressed the importance of peer review. She noted that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped.
  • Elizabeth Graham: Stated that the “problem” is not discovering new sites, as most Maya sites are known but unexplored. She highlighted that local communities are often aware of sites and that funding is the bigger obstacle to research.

item.title: Semantic Diff Tool for Formal Policies and AI Code
item.description:
Semantic Diff Tool for Formal Policies and AI Code

When reviewing code, you start with a diff. However, comparing two 3,000-line files by eye is difficult. Formal policies are even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. A new development introduces a semantic diff to solve this problem.

🔍 Overview

A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. This approach addresses the limitations of standard text diffs, where reordering conjuncts, swapping the arguments of an equality, or using an equivalent predicate can cause much of a file to appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and, can get lost in that noise.

⚙️ How it works

The engine computes this diff using anti-unification, which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. This method is based on Plotkin’s 1970 paper.

  • Engine Structure: The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal.
  • Justification: Algebraic laws and domain rules justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal.
  • Equivalence: If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules.
  • Completeness: When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found.

🚀 Use Cases

The primary use case is autoformalization, which translates natural language into a formal language.

  • Target Languages: SMT-LIB (standard input for Z3 and cvc5), Cedar, Dogwood, OpenShell, and Common Expression Language (CEL).
  • LLM Generation: A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from prose.
  • Comparison Process: Run the model twice to produce two different formalizations. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ.
  • Candidate Generation: Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature.

💡 Benefits

  • Analogy: This is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy, described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024).
  • Information Preservation: For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information.
  • Counterexamples: Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other.
  • Review Visibility: When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review.
  • Operator Handling: The reordering doesn’t appear in the result because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Adds Web Search API for AI Agents
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Adds Web Search API for AI Agents

AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count.

🌐 Overview

The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use.

⚙️ Key Details

  • AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third‑party search engine.
  • Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query.
  • Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range.
  • There’s no search API key to store or rotate.
  • Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway.
  • For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API.
  • The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget.
  • It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph, the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents, which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression.
  • The Web Search API needs one IAM action on one resource that AWS owns, so the statement is the same in every account.
  • Web Search and model calls are billed per use.
  • One run of the watch makes at most 12 searches.

🧩 Use Case: The Watch

Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control.

In our test, the three branches finished in 36 seconds, against 99 seconds one after another. A run starts the graph with the watchlist and the watch window. Inside each branch, the agent calls an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock. The model decides what to search for and, at the end, produces structured findings.

The branch’s search tool adds the date window and the blocklist to each query. It calls the Web Search API with a request signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4). Each branch keeps only findings that its sources support and that fall inside the window. The examples use the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1).

The watch can’t let the model choose the date window, the trusted sources, or the number of searches. Every search carries the blocklist and the date floor, and a model’s own arguments could only narrow them.

🚀 Availability

On AWS Lambda, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, your agent calls the API with its execution role. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results.

item.title: Mobile AI Factory Automates SLM Tuning for Android Devices
item.description:
Mobile AI Factory Automates SLM Tuning for Android Devices

A new system titled “Mobile AI Factory” was submitted on November 10, 2026. It automates the creation of specialized, quantized Small Language Models (SLMs) for Android devices.

🔍 Overview

Mobile AI Factory is an agentic system designed to build fine-tuned, quantized SLMs for specific tasks and phones. These models run locally, preserving user data privacy and functioning without connectivity.

🧩 How it works

The system uses an orchestrator LLM to decide whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples. It employs fixed rules to roll back changes that negatively impact accuracy. The search process moves from small to large models and adapts its accuracy goals during the search.

⚙️ Key details

  • Search Strategy: Searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations.
  • Adaptation: Adapts its accuracy goal as it searches.
  • Hardware Awareness: Uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends.
  • Comparison: Without phone measurements, Claude Opus 5.5 misses requirements in 25% of easy and moderate cases and 60% of hard cases.

📊 Evaluation

The system was evaluated on ten tasks and four Android phones.

Evaluation Scope Details
Tasks 10
Devices 4 Android phones
  • Performance: On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperformed two five-shot frontier models on five tasks (by up to 0.34) and matched them on three more.
  • Efficiency: The search came within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants on an entity extraction task, while using 19x less GPU time.
  • Hardware Dependency: The best configuration changes across phones.

🚀 Availability

Code for Mobile AI Factory is available at the provided URL.

item.title: Meta Updates Terms to Allow AI Training on Associated Websites
item.description:
Meta Updates Terms to Allow AI Training on Associated Websites

Meta has updated its terms of service to grant itself permission to crawl and scrape websites associated with business accounts for AI training. The new terms, which go into effect on October 30, allow Meta to use outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products.

🔍 Overview

The policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. It allows Meta to crawl all websites ‘associated’ with a business account. This includes domains, web pages, or URLs that are made available through the business’s use of Meta’s products and services.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Authorization: The terms authorize Meta to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, crawlers, and user agents) to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl domains associated with products or services.
  • Usage: Meta may use any content from such domains to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of its Meta Company Products and services.
  • Enforcement: Businesses that do not agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

🧩 Legal and Industry Context

  • Robots.txt: Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts states there is “no change to how Meta uses web crawlers” and claims content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences.
  • Expert Analysis: Legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions, like a site’s robots.txt file. This could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers.
  • Existing Deals: Meta has followed OpenAI in striking AI licensing deals with CNN, Fox News, USA Today, and People Inc., but these new terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content.
  • Professor Quote: James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, tells Nieman Lab that for news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves.

💡 Why It Matters

  • News Sites: The new policy may allow Meta to train AI on news sites for free.
  • Meta’s Stance: Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, writes in a post on X that this change isn’t meant to target news sites, stating the update is designed to pull accurate information about products for sale on third‑party websites when making on‑platform ad and content recommendations.
  • Cost Implications: Last month, Meta launched a new Meta One subscription that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. Nieman Lab notes that “Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free.”

item.title: ABU Hosts Hands-On AI Agents Training for Staffing Professionals
item.description:
ABU Hosts Hands-On AI Agents Training for Staffing Professionals

The Association of Temporary Employment Agencies (ABU) is organizing a hands-on training on October 12, 2026, focusing on AI Agents. This workshop aims to move beyond basic text generation and summarization, teaching participants how to automate complete processes and connect various systems and tools.

🔍 Overview

AI agents allow for the automation of complete processes and the delegation of tasks. The training goes deeper than using tools like ChatGPT or Copilot, focusing on converting recurring work into smart, automated workflows. Examples include agents that process incoming emails, structure information, and prepare draft responses, as well as processes where different systems collaborate.

📅 Key Details

Attribute Details
Date 12 October 2026
Time 09:00 – 17:00
Location ABU
Cost € 200 excl. btw
Trainer Wahbé Rezek en Krista Plat

🧩 What You Will Learn

  • What AI agents are and what is currently possible
  • Which processes within your organization are suitable for automation
  • How to work with no-code automation tools
  • Step-by-step construction of your own AI workflow or agent
  • Connecting diverse tools and data sources
  • Safety, reliability, and human control
  • Practical examples and use cases relevant to the staffing industry

🛠️ Requirements

  • Experience: The training is intended for people with some experience in AI who wish to deepen their knowledge.
  • Technical: Programming knowledge is not necessary, but basic digital skills and enthusiasm to experiment are required.
  • Tools: A paid subscription to ChatGPT or Claude is required. Participants should bring their own laptop to apply what they learn directly.

📝 Registration

  • Action: Register easily via the button.
  • Data: By registering, you agree to share your name, job title, email address, and employer with the trainers.
  • Cancellation: If you are unable to attend, please cancel at least two weeks (28 September) in advance or arrange for a colleague to attend via ledenservice@abu.nl.
  • Access: A paid subscription to ChatGPT or Claude is required to participate.

item.title: Meta Launches Proprietary Multimodal Model Muse Wonder
item.description:
Meta Launches Proprietary Multimodal Model Muse Wonder

Meta officially released Muse Wonder on October 12, 2026, introducing a new multimodal AI model to its growing artificial intelligence portfolio. The proprietary system marks Meta’s latest effort to compete in the multimodal AI space, where models process both text and visual information.

🔍 Overview

Muse Wonder processes both text and image inputs, positioning it alongside other multimodal systems like GPT-4 Vision and Gemini. The model’s architecture enables it to understand visual context and generate responses that incorporate both language understanding and image interpretation. The system reportedly employs transformer-based architectures optimized for joint text-image processing.

🧩 Capabilities

According to Meta, Muse Wonder can analyze photographs, diagrams, charts, and other visual content while maintaining conversational context. The system’s multimodal design allows developers to build applications that require simultaneous processing of text and visual data.

  • Visual Analysis: Analyzes photographs, diagrams, and charts.
  • Contextual Response: Generates responses incorporating visual interpretation and language understanding.
  • Document Analysis: Processes text and graphics appearing together.
  • Use Cases: Content moderation, visual question answering, and image captioning.

⚙️ Licensing & Strategy

Muse Wonder operates under a proprietary license, signaling a strategic shift in the company’s AI distribution approach. This decision represents a departure from Meta’s recent trend of releasing open-weight models.

Model Licensing Approach
Llama Series Permissive licensing allowing modification and free deployment.
Muse Wonder Proprietary license restricting usage to Meta’s controlled infrastructure.

Industry analysts suggest the proprietary approach may reflect Meta’s assessment of multimodal AI’s competitive value. Visual understanding capabilities require substantial compute resources and training data, potentially justifying tighter control over distribution and monetization. This decision also aligns with practices from OpenAI and Anthropic, which maintain proprietary access to their most advanced multimodal systems.

🚀 Availability

Officially launched on October 12, 2026, Muse Wonder became available through Meta’s AI platform infrastructure. The release follows months of internal testing and represents Meta’s continued investment in multimodal artificial intelligence research.

Meta has not disclosed detailed pricing information but confirmed the model operates through API access similar to other proprietary AI services. The October launch positions Muse Wonder in a competitive market where OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and other major players have already deployed multimodal systems. While Meta has not published detailed technical specifications, parameter count and training data composition remain undisclosed.

item.title: Study Introduces Structural-Complexity Index for Prompt Evaluation
item.description:
Study Introduces Structural-Complexity Index for Prompt Evaluation

A new study introduces a six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation. The research evaluates 105,000 generations across 21 models to analyze performance thresholds and reliability regimes.

🔍 Overview

The contribution is a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes. The index is scored separately from correctness.

🧩 Methodology

  • Dataset: The study selects 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater rubric.
  • Raters: Four out-of-panel LLM raters rescore the locked prompts, giving 19,997 score rows.
  • Generations: The study evaluates 21 models per prompt, yielding 105,000 generations.
  • Reliability: Composite inter-rater reliability is ICC = 0.872 on the 4,998 prompts with all four ratings.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • Performance Breakpoints:
    • Unadjusted mean-pooled analysis shows a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 13.75.
    • Task-type fixed effects shift the breakpoint to 10.75.
    • A construction-frame control shifts it to 8.50.
  • Model-Specific Fits: The analysis includes 16 upward and five downward changes.
  • Complexity Analysis: Among zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity, 28.5% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity at most 10.

📊 Reliability and Calibration

  • Human agreement is moderate and rater-dependent on a disagreement-enriched calibration set.
  • Paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve score ordering.

💡 Conclusion

Overidentification tests reject the joint restrictions on the six dimensions. The composite is treated as an index, and no causal interpretation is made of the 2SLS estimates.

item.title: AI Agent Skill 'Ponytail' Reduces Code by 54% While Staying Safe
item.description:
AI Agent Skill ‘Ponytail’ Reduces Code by 54% While Staying Safe

A new AI agent skill, “ponytail,” is designed to make an AI agent think like the laziest senior developer in the room. The philosophy behind the development is that the best code is the code you never wrote.

🧩 The Persona

The skill is visualized as a developer with a long ponytail and oval glasses who has been at the company longer than version control. When shown fifty lines of code, he looks at them, says nothing, and replaces them with one. The ponytail is the only arm that cuts every metric, and the only one that stays fully safe while doing it.

⚙️ Methodology & Results

The honest measurement involves a real agent doing real work: a headless Claude Code session editing tiangolo’s full-stack-fastapi-template (a real FastAPI + React repo), scored on the git diff it leaves behind. Twelve feature tickets were tested with the same agent with and without the skill, using Haiku 4.5.

The cut is biggest where there is a real over-build trap. For example, a date picker was reduced from 404 lines to 23, and a color picker from 287 to 23, because the agent reaches for a native <input> instead of a component. This approach keeps every safety guard while a bare “write one-liners” prompt drops one.

📊 Performance Benchmarks

Five everyday tasks were tested across three models and three arms (no skill, caveman, ponytail), with ten runs reported as the median.

Model Code Reduction Cost Reduction Cost Reduction Time Reduction Safety
ponytail -54% -22% -20% -27% 100%
caveman (terse-prose control) -20% +7% +3% +2% 100%
“YAGNI + one-liners” prompt -33% -14% -21% -30% 95%

Full method, per-task tables, and limitations are available at benchmarks/results/2026-06-18-agentic.md. More survivors in examples/.

item.title: Claude Agent SDK vs LangGraph: Control Flow Philosophies
item.description:
Claude Agent SDK vs LangGraph: Control Flow Philosophies

The debate between the Claude Agent SDK and LangGraph is often framed as a product comparison, but it is actually a comparison of two philosophies regarding who should be responsible for an agent’s control flow.

🔍 Overview

The Claude Agent SDK and LangGraph offer different approaches to building AI agents. One hands you a loop, while the other hands you a box of primitives to draw a graph.

🧩 The Claude Agent SDK (The Loop Philosophy)

The Claude Agent SDK hands you a loop. It already knows how to plan, call a tool, read the result, and decide what to do next because it is the same loop that runs Claude Code.

  • How it works: You import it, define your tools, point it at a task, and the loop does the rest: plans, calls tools, reads results, and keeps going until it is finished or you stop it.
  • Capabilities: You get code execution, file manipulation, bash, web browsing, and MCP tool integrations out of the box.
  • Constraints: You do not get a say in how the loop behaves. The retry semantics, the way it decides what to do next, and the order it approaches a problem are all decided. Additionally, every task runs on a Claude model, making it Claude-only.

🧩 LangGraph (The Graph Philosophy)

LangGraph hands you a box of primitives and expects you to draw the graph yourself. You declare nodes, edges, and a shared state schema, and the framework executes the graph until a node returns END.

  • Features: You can write specific logic, such as a node that fans out to five parallel branches, joins them, checks a condition, and loops back twice.
  • Execution: Checkpointers provide durable execution by saving state to persistent storage after every logical step, so a crash or a restart resumes from the last checkpoint. Interrupts allow for real human-in-the-loop capabilities by pausing the graph at a specific node.
  • Tech Stack: It is model-agnostic, supports Python and JavaScript, and plugs into LangSmith for tracing and LangGraph Platform for deployment.
  • Maturity: It is the most widely adopted thing in this space by a wide margin, and that maturity is worth something on its own.

⚙️ Performance and Availability

The Claude Agent SDK is built for speed with ~10ms latency, even under load. It handles 350+ RPS on just 1 vCPU without needing tuning. It is production-ready with full enterprise support.

💡 Which Approach Fits?

Both approaches are defensible. The choice depends on a question most teams answer too late: does your agent actually need a custom topology, or does it just need to work?

item.title: Zacks Rank System and Adobe Stock Analysis
item.description:
Zacks Rank System and Adobe Stock Analysis

The Zacks Rank serves as a timeliness indicator for stocks over the next 1 to 3 months. It is a complementary set of indicators to use alongside the Style Scores.

⚙️ How it works

The scores are based on the trading styles of Value, Growth, and Momentum. There is a VGM Score (‘V’ for Value, ‘G’ for Growth and ‘M’ for Momentum), which combines the weighted average of the individual style scores into one score. Within each Score, stocks are graded into five groups: A, B, C, D and F.

📊 Industry Analysis

The Zacks Industry Rank assigns a rating to each of the 265 X (Expanded) Industries based on their average Zacks Rank. The industry with the best average Zacks Rank would be considered the top industry (1 out of 265), which would place it in the top 1% of Zacks Ranked Industries. Conversely, the industry with the worst average Zacks Rank (265 out of 265) would place in the bottom 1%.

📈 Adobe Stock Performance

For their last quarter, Adobe (ADBE) reported earnings of $6.13 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $6.08 per share. This reflects a positive earnings surprise of 0.82%.

In the earnings report for the quarter ending in August 2024, Adobe Inc. (ADBE) announced earnings of $4.65 per share versus the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.53 per share, representing a surprise of 2.65%.

Look out for ADBE’s next earnings release expected on December 09, 2026. For the next earning release, we expect the company to report earnings of $6.30 per share, reflecting a year-over-year increase of 14.55%.

📚 Research Tools

The Zacks Equity Research reports, or ZER for short, are our in-house, independently produced research reports. The ever popular one-page Snapshot reports are generated for virtually every single Zacks Ranked stock.
